meta.title: Who really said "A penny saved is a penny earned"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Franklin. He wrote "A penny saved is twopence clear" (1737). The "earned" wording is an anonymous English proverb, first documented in 1804.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A penny saved is a penny earned'?
meta.ogDescription: Franklin never wrote "earned." His real 1737 maxim was "A penny saved is twopence clear" — and the proverb itself is a century older than him.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — an anonymous English proverb
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · ancestor forms in print from 1633 · the ‘earned’ wording from 1804
answer.sourceLine: Franklin never wrote “earned.” What he actually printed, in the “Hints for those that would be Rich” column of Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1737, was a different and stronger maxim: “A penny saved is twopence clear.” The “a penny earned” wording is first documented in 1804 — fourteen years after Franklin’s death — and even there it is introduced as “that good old saying,” so its coiner is unknown.
answer.confidenceText: Franklin’s real 1737 wording is confirmed against a scanned edition; the “earned” variant is traced to an 1804 printing that already calls it proverbial.

source.heading: The earliest documented “earned”

docMeta.dd: “A penny saved is a penny earned” — anonymous English proverb
“A penny saved is twopence clear” — Poor Richard’s Almanack (1737)
“A Penny saved is a Penny got” — The Spectator, No. 2 (2 March 1711)

source.excerpt: I have reason to fear, that too many masters of ships forget that good old saying, “A penny saved is a penny earned”.
trail: c. 1633 — the ancestor. George Herbert’s Outlandish Proverbs gives “A penny spar’d is twice got”; Thomas Fuller (c. 1661) has “a penny saved is a penny gained” and Edward Ravenscroft’s Canterbury Guests (1695) “A penny sav’d, is a penny got,” per The Phrase Finder ↗.

1711 — in The Spectator. In Richard Steele’s No. 2 (2 March 1711), the merchant Sir Andrew Freeport “abounds in several frugal Maxims, amongst which the greatest Favourite is, ‘A Penny saved is a Penny got’” — already a quoted maxim, not Steele’s coinage (full text ↗).

1732 — Franklin quotes it. Writing as “Celia Single” in The Pennsylvania Gazette (24 July 1732), Franklin has a husband say “you know a penny sav’d is a penny got, A pin a day is a groat a year, every little makes a muckle” — borrowing, not inventing (Smyth, Writings, vol. 2 ↗).

1737 — Franklin rewrites it. In “Hints for those that would be Rich,” after a passage on ready money versus credit, he prints his own sharper version: “A penny saved is twopence clear. A pin a-day is a groat a-year. Save and have. Every little makes a mickle” (scanned text, under the head “Poor Richard for 1737” ↗).
1804 — “earned” appears. The familiar wording surfaces in Joseph Huddart’s Swansea Harbour report, p. 13, already labelled “that good old saying” (Wiktionary citation ↗).
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest documented appearance of the familiar wording, and it is already secondhand: Huddart introduces it as “that good old saying,” not as anything of his own. Franklin had died fourteen years earlier, and his own version of the maxim used neither “earned” nor “a penny” on the second half — he wrote “twopence clear.”

sourceLink.text: Wiktionary: a penny saved is a penny earned (with the 1804 citation)

source.rightsNote: Every documented carrier of this wording is comfortably out of copyright in the United States: the 1804 Huddart report in which it first appears, along with its antecedents — The Spectator No. 2 (1711) and Poor Richard’s Almanack (1737) — were all published long before 1931. The proverb itself is anonymous and traditional, with no identifiable author or estate to hold a claim. Note that the rights status is settled here despite the authorship being unknown, not because of it.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.kicker: The man who gets the credit
author.heading: So what did Franklin actually write?
author.bio: Franklin ran Poor Richard’s Almanack from 1733 to 1758, and his genius there was editorial rather than original — he openly harvested existing English proverbs and sharpened them. As he admitted in the 1758 preface, the sayings contained “the wisdom of many ages and nations,” not just his own. The thrift maxim is a case in point: he quoted the common version in 1732, then rewrote it in 1737 into something sharper. The line the world remembers is neither of those.

copyAttribution: "A penny saved is a penny earned" — an anonymous English proverb; earliest known printing 1804 (Joseph Huddart, Swansea Harbour, p. 13), where it is already called "that good old saying." Frequently misattributed to Benjamin Franklin, who instead wrote "A penny saved is twopence clear" in Poor Richard's Almanack (1737).

misattribution.heading: How Franklin got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is the rare misquote that is wrong three times over: wrong wording, wrong author, and wrong century. Here is what each part of the popular story gets wrong.

items.why: The Franklin Institute lists this among things Franklin never said ↗, giving his actual 1737 wording as “A penny saved is two pence clear.” The scanned 1737 text bears this out: under the running head “Poor Richard for 1737” it reads “A penny saved is twopence clear. A pin a-day is a groat a-year.” ↗

The Phrase Finder traces ancestor forms well before Franklin’s birth — George Herbert’s Outlandish Proverbs (c. 1633), “A penny spar’d is twice got”; Thomas Fuller (c. 1661), “a penny saved is a penny gained”; and Edward Ravenscroft’s Canterbury Guests (1695), “A penny sav’d, is a penny got” — and reports “no known record” of Franklin originating it ↗.

In his 24 July 1732 Pennsylvania Gazette letter signed “Celia Single,” Franklin writes “you know a penny sav’d is a penny got” ↗. The words you know mark it as a saying his readers already knew — it had run in Steele’s Spectator No. 2 in 1711 ↗ as a merchant’s “greatest Favourite” maxim.

The Phrase Finder points to a US cent token of about 1863 carrying Franklin’s image on one side and the proverb on the other ↗ — which it calls “probably the most literal coining of a phrase.” Face and phrase travelled together from there.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying belongs to nobody. Its earliest documented appearance in the familiar “earned” form is an 1804 report on Swansea Harbour ↗ — fourteen years after Franklin’s death — and even there the writer calls it “that good old saying,” meaning it was already anonymous and old by then.
